did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter describes the blowing of a trumpet in Zion as a warning, because the day of the Lord is near and is portrayed as a day that causes the inhabitants of the land to tremble.

Did you know? The day of the Lord is described as a day of darkness, clouds, and gloom. At the same time, an immense army is described—unlike anything that has existed before or will exist in the future.
Did you know? The enemy army is described as organized and disciplined: its soldiers run like warriors, advance each along his own path, and do not deviate from their course.
Did you know? The description of the assault emphasizes the army’s power: it moves through the city, runs along the wall, climbs into houses, and enters through the windows like a thief.
Did you know? A cosmic upheaval is described before the army: the earth quakes, the heavens tremble, and the sun, moon, and stars darken their light.

Did you know? The call to repentance emphasizes inner change, not merely outward change: “Rend your hearts and not your garments,” because the Lord is gracious, compassionate, and abundant in kindness.

Did you know? The solemn assembly for repentance is intended for the entire people: the elderly, children, and even nursing infants are gathered, and the bridegroom and bride are called to leave their chamber and wedding canopy.

Did you know? The priests pray between the porch and the altar and ask the Lord to have compassion on His people, so that Israel will not be subjected to disgrace and the nations will not ask, “Where is their God?”
Did you know? After the calamity, agricultural renewal is promised: the early and late rains will fall and help restore blessing to the land.

Did you know? The Lord promises to restore to the people the years damaged by the various kinds of locusts—the cutting locust, swarming locust, hopping locust, and destroying locust—and to restore abundance and satisfaction.
